newsitem.title: CANADA: Union urges members to approve Canadian plan.
newsitem.headline: Union urges members to approve Canadian plan.

text.p: The Canadian Union of Public Employees, one of two unions earlier this week rejecting Canadian Airlines Corp's survival plan, said on Friday it would urge members to support it in a December 7 vote.

CUPE president Judy Darcy said in a phone interview that union leaders agreed to the plan after British Columbia Premier Glen Clark, in an early morning meeting, agreed to increase the province's contribution to the carrier's financial restructuring package by C$3.1 million.
"We will be recommending acceptance to our membership," Darcy said.
CUPE represents 2,700 flight attendants at Canadian.

B.C.'s move will mean workers earning less than C$25,000 a year will not be forced to take reductions in pay. The new earnings threshold compares with a previous level of C$23,000, set when the governments of Canada, Alberta and B.C. agreed to concessions earlier this week.
"We have agreed to increase our contribution by C$3.1 million and this is particularly to address the low-wage workers," Clark said.
Darcy conceded that the C$25,000 threshold was lower than the one her union had demanded as late as Thursday.

"But it's a whole lot more than where we were a few weeks ago," she said, pointing out the carrier's previous demands for across-the-board 10-percent pay cuts and its rejection of government involvement.

She said Canadian Transport Minister David Anderson agreed in an earlier meeting to study the ruling Liberal government's air transport policy, but did not promise re-regulation, which both CUPE and the Canadian Auto Workers have called for.
CUPE is pressing the government to start public discussions on the best way to ensure the financial viability of both major airlines in Canada, Darcy said.
Canadian Airlines, however, still faces a hurdle with the Canadian Auto Workers -- the one remaining holdout union.

CAW president Buzz Hargrove has come under intense pressure from politicians as well as rank-and-file members within his own union to allow the CAW's 3,700 airline workers to vote on Canadian's plan. -- Reuters Calgary Bureau 403 531-1624
